prompt: `readlink /proc/<pid>/ns/net` gives `net:[4026532266]` for the container and `net:[4026531833]` for Ana's shell. What does that tell her?
hint: When do two processes show the same number?

choices.text: They are in different network namespaces
choices.why: Right. The same namespace shows the same number; these differ.

choices.text: The container's network is faster
choices.why: The numbers identify namespaces; they measure nothing.

choices.text: The container has 4026532266 network interfaces
choices.why: It had two, `lo` and `eth0`; the number names the namespace.

choices.text: The two processes share a network but have different firewalls
choices.why: Sharing a namespace would show the same number.

prompt: `lsns` showed the container's `user` namespace shared with 89 host processes. What follows for a process running as root inside it?

choices.text: It is an unprivileged user on the host, because Docker remaps root by default
choices.why: That remapping is a user namespace, and this container has none of its own.

choices.text: It cannot run, since root is forbidden in containers by the kernel
choices.why: It ran: `sleep 600` as root.

choices.text: It is the host's root, held back only by the other walls
choices.why: Right. Lesson 21 is about the other walls and adding this one.

choices.text: It belongs to user `kthreadd`
choices.why: `kthreadd` is just the first process listed in that shared namespace.

prompt: On the host, `ls /sys/class/net` lists a `veth…` interface that appeared with the container. What is it?

choices.text: A second network card Docker added to the machine
choices.why: No hardware was added; it is virtual.

choices.text: One end of a virtual cable
choices.why: Right: the host's end, and the container's `eth0` is the other. Lesson 23 follows it to the `docker0` bridge.

choices.text: The container's loopback, seen from outside
choices.why: The container's `lo` stays inside its namespace.

choices.text: A VPN Docker opens to Docker Hub
choices.why: Nothing about it reaches outside the machine.

prompt: Ana runs `sudo nsenter --target $PID --uts --net sh -c "hostname; ip -brief addr"`. Whose files does the `ip` program come from?
hint: Which namespaces were entered, and which were not?

choices.text: The host's: the mount namespace was not entered
choices.why: Right. Only UTS and network were entered, so files and programs stayed the host's.

choices.text: The container's, because `nsenter` copies the program in
choices.why: Nothing is copied; the program is found in the filesystem of whichever mount namespace the process is in.

choices.text: Alpine's busybox, which is why it printed `-brief` output
choices.why: Alpine's `ip` refused `-brief` in this very lesson; this one is the host's iproute2.

choices.text: Neither; `nsenter` has a built-in `ip`
choices.why: `nsenter` only joins namespaces and runs the program it is given.

prompt: Match each namespace to what it gives a container its own copy of.
right_distractors: The amount of memory it may use

prompt: `cpu.cfs_quota_us` is 50000 and `cpu.cfs_period_us` is 100000. What does the container get?
hint: Divide one by the other, and think in time.

choices.text: Processor number 0 out of the four
choices.why: The limit is time, not a particular processor.

choices.text: Half the machine's four processors
choices.why: That would be `--cpus 2`. 50000 of 100000 is half of one processor's time.

choices.text: 50 ms of CPU time in every 100 ms period
choices.why: Right: half of one processor's worth of time, which is `--cpus 0.5`.

choices.text: A 50% chance of being scheduled
choices.why: Scheduling is not a lottery here; the quota is a fixed budget per period.

prompt: Ana started a container with `--memory 64m`. What number does `memory.limit_in_bytes` hold?
A container exits with code 137 and `docker inspect` shows `OOMKilled=false`. What is the best reading?

choices.text: It ran out of memory, and Docker recorded it the wrong way
choices.why: That would show `OOMKilled=true`.

choices.text: A `SIGKILL` from something other than the memory limit
choices.why: Right. 137 says signal 9; `false` says it was not the memory limit.

choices.text: It exited normally after running for 137 seconds
choices.why: An exit code is not a duration.

choices.text: It hit the limit on the number of processes it may start
choices.why: A process limit refuses a fork; it does not kill the container.

prompt: Match each limit to what happens when a container reaches it.
hint: One refuses, one kills, one makes you wait.

pairs.right: A new process cannot be created
The kernel kills a process with `SIGKILL`
The processes wait for the next period

right_distractors: Docker restarts the container with a higher limit

prompt: On a cgroup v2 machine, where would Ana look for the memory limit of a container?

choices.text: In a file called `memory.max`
choices.why: Right: in the container's single cgroup directory. Same limit, another file name, one directory for every controller.

choices.text: `memory.limit_in_bytes` under `/sys/fs/cgroup/memory/docker/`
choices.why: That is the v1 layout the lab machine shows.

choices.text: In `/proc/meminfo` inside the container
choices.why: Lesson 2 showed that file reports the host's memory.

choices.text: Nowhere; v2 has no memory limits
choices.why: It has them, with a different file name.

prompt: After `rm /etc/motd` inside the container, what does the upper layer hold at `etc/motd`?
hint: Look at the first character of the `ls -l` line.

choices.text: Nothing; the file was removed from Alpine's layer
choices.why: Lower layers are never written; the original is still in snapshot 110.

choices.text: A copy of `motd` whose contents were replaced by a note saying it was deleted
choices.why: It is not a regular file at all.

choices.text: A whiteout: a character device numbered `0, 0` that hides the file below
choices.why: Right. Overlayfs hides the lower file when it sees the whiteout first.

choices.text: A symbolic link to `/dev/null`
choices.why: The `ls -l` line starts with `c`, a character device, not `l`.

prompt: An image ships a 2 GB file, and a container appends one line to it. What does the upper layer gain?
hint: What has to happen before a lower file can change?

choices.text: One line
choices.why: Lower layers cannot be changed, so the file has to be copied up before it is written.

choices.text: A whole 2 GB copy, with the line added
choices.why: Right. The first write copies the file up, and the copy is what changes.

choices.text: Nothing, because the write is refused
choices.why: The write succeeds; it lands on a copy.

choices.text: A link to the original in the image's layer
choices.why: A link could not hold the change; overlayfs copies the file.

prompt: Which files did Docker write into the small layer between Alpine's and the container's own? Choose all that apply.
hint: Things that differ per container but are not the program's writes.

choices.text: `etc/hostname`
choices.why: Yes: the name the container was given.

choices.text: `etc/hosts`
choices.why: Yes, along with the DNS settings in `etc/resolv.conf`.

choices.text: `.dockerenv`
choices.why: Yes: an empty marker file.

choices.text: `tmp/new.txt`
choices.why: That was Ana's write; it is in the upper layer.

choices.text: `bin/busybox`
choices.why: That comes from Alpine's own layer.

prompt: Order the layers of `web` from the top of the stack, which overlayfs reads first, to the bottom.
A container's application starts 500 threads and then fails with "Resource temporarily unavailable". The machine has plenty of memory. Which mechanism stopped it?

choices.text: The PID namespace
choices.why: A namespace changes what a process sees, not how many it may have.

choices.text: The memory cgroup
choices.why: That kills; this refused.

choices.text: The pids cgroup's limit
choices.why: Right. Each thread counts against `pids.max`, and the refusal is that error.

choices.text: Overlayfs, which allows a limited number of open files
choices.why: That would be a different error, and the filesystem has no thread limit.

prompt: Match each question about a container to the kernel feature that answers it.

pairs.left: Where do its files come from?

prompt: A common way for a program to tell it is running in a Docker container is to check for an empty file at the root of the filesystem called ___.
hint: Docker writes it into the per-container layer.
